title: Arbitrary Arguments
objective: Accept any number of positional arguments with *args and any number of named arguments with **kwargs.

sourceAlignment.title: Python Crash Course, 3rd Edition
sourceAlignment.author: Eric Matthes
sourceAlignment.chapterTitle: Passing an Arbitrary Number of Arguments
sourceAlignment.note: Alignment metadata only. Lesson prose and exercises are original Code Forge material.

paragraphs: Sometimes you don't know in advance how many values a function needs to accept. A parameter written with a single * in front, like *items, collects every extra positional argument into one tuple that the function body can use.
You can still mix a normal required parameter with an arbitrary one — the required parameter must come first, and *args soaks up whatever is left.

Inside the function, the collected values behave like any other sequence: you can check how many there are with len(), or loop over them once loops are covered. For now, just know *args gathers them into a single tuple named whatever you called it.

A parameter written with two stars in front, like **details, works the same way but for keyword arguments instead: it collects every extra name=value argument into a single dictionary, with each keyword becoming a key. You can mix all three kinds in one function, but the order in the def line is fixed: regular parameters first, then *args, then **kwargs.
explanation.rule: *name collects extra positional arguments into a tuple; **name collects extra keyword arguments into a dictionary.

examples.title: Collecting Extra Arguments
examples.note: customer takes the first argument; every argument after it is gathered into the items tuple, which here has length 3.

examples.title: Collecting Extra Keyword Arguments
examples.code:
def print_profile(username, **details):
    print(username)
    print(details)

print_profile("ada99", rank="apprentice", years=2)
examples.note: username takes the first argument; every keyword argument after it is gathered into the details dictionary, in the order they were passed.

checks.question: def total(*values): — what is values inside the function when you call total(1, 2, 3)?

feedback.correct: Correct — *values collects all positional arguments into a single tuple.
feedback.incorrect: *values gathers every positional argument into one tuple, not just the first or last.

checks.question: def profile(**info): — what is info inside the function when you call profile(rank="smith", years=5)?
options: Two separate variables, rank and years.
A SyntaxError, since profile has no regular parameters.

feedback.correct: Correct — **info collects every keyword argument into a single dictionary.
feedback.incorrect: **info gathers every name=value argument into one dictionary, keyed by the argument names.

assignment.title: Count the Order
assignment.brief: Write order_summary(customer, *items, **details) that prints customer, then prints len(items), then prints the details dictionary.
requirements: Print customer, then print len(items), then print details.
assignment.starterCode:
def order_summary(customer, *items, **details):
    # Print customer, then len(items), then details.
    pass

order_summary("Ada", "hammer", "tongs", "ingot", gift_wrap=True, rush=False)
assignment.solutionCode:
def order_summary(customer, *items, **details):
    print(customer)
    print(len(items))
    print(details)

order_summary("Ada", "hammer", "tongs", "ingot", gift_wrap=True, rush=False)
assignment.testHarness:
# ---- Code Forge validation ----
import io, contextlib
_cf_buf = io.StringIO()
with contextlib.redirect_stdout(_cf_buf):
    order_summary("Ada", "hammer", "tongs", "ingot", gift_wrap=True, rush=False)
_cf_result = _cf_buf.getvalue()
print("__CF_TEST_OUTPUT__")
print(repr(_cf_result))
assignment.outputCheckLabel: order_summary(...) prints Ada, then 3, then the details dictionary

hints: customer is a normal parameter; *items collects positional extras; **details collects keyword extras.
len(items) tells you how many extra positional arguments were passed.
Three items were passed after 'Ada', so len(items) should be 3.
print(details) shows the whole dictionary at once — you don't need to loop over it or pick out keys.
